title: Weighing scale
description: Instrument to measure the weight of an object
wiki_lead:
A scale or balance is a device used to measure weight or mass. These are also known as mass scales, weight scales, mass balances, massometers, and weight balances.
The traditional scale consists of two plates or bowls suspended at equal distances from a fulcrum. One plate holds an object of unknown mass (or weight), while objects of known mass or weight, called weights, are added to the other plate until mechanical equilibrium is achieved and the plates level off, which happens when the masses on the two plates are equal. The perfect scale rests at neutral. A spring scale will make use of a spring of known stiffness to determine mass (or weight). Suspending a certain mass will extend the spring by a certain amount depending on the spring's stiffness (or spring constant). The heavier the object, the more the spring stretches, as described in Hooke's law. Other types of scales making use of different physical principles also exist.
Some scales can be calibrated to read in units of force (weight) such as newtons instead of units of mass such as kilograms. Scales and balances are widely used in commerce, as many products are sold and packaged by mass.

History

The balance scale is such a simple device that its usage likely far predates the evidence. What has allowed archaeologists to link artifacts to weighing scales are the stones for determining absolute mass. The balance scale itself was probably used to determine relative mass long before absolute mass.
The oldest attested evidence for the existence of weighing scales dates to the Fourth Dynasty of Egypt, with deben balance weights, from the reign of Sneferu (c. 2600 BC) excavated, though earlier usage has been proposed. Carved stones bearing marks denoting mass and the Egyptian hieroglyphic symbol for gold have been discovered, which suggests that Egyptian merchants had been using an established system of mass measurement to catalog gold shipments or gold mine yields. Although no actual scales from this era have survived, many sets of weighing stones as well as murals depicting the use of balance scales suggest widespread usage.
Examples, dating  c. 2400–1800 BC, have also been found in the Indus River valley. Uniform, polished stone cubes discovered in early settlements were probably used as mass-setting stones in balance scales. Although the cubes bear no markings, their masses are multiples of a common denominator. The cubes are made of many different kinds of stones with varying densities. Clearly their mass, not their size or other characteristics, was a factor in sculpting these cubes.
In China, the earliest weighing balance excavated was from a tomb of the state of Chu of the Chinese Warring States period dating back to the 3rd to 4th century BC in Mount Zuojiagong near Changsha, Hunan. The balance was made of wood and used bronze masses.
Variations on the balance scale, including devices like the cheap and inaccurate bismar (unequal-armed scales), began to see common usage by c. 400 BC by many small merchants and their customers. A plethora of scale varieties each boasting advantages and improvements over one another appear throughout recorded history, with such great inventors as Leonardo da Vinci lending a personal hand in their development.
Even with all the advances in weighing scale design and development, all scales until the seventeenth century AD were variations on the balance scale.  The standardization of the weights used – and ensuring traders used the correct weights – was a considerable preoccupation of governments throughout this time.

The original form of a balance consisted of a beam with a fulcrum at its center. For highest accuracy, the fulcrum would consist of a sharp V-shaped pivot seated in a shallower V-shaped bearing. To determine the mass of the object, a combination of reference masses was hung on one end of the beam while the object of unknown mass was hung on the other end (see balance and steelyard balance). grok_lead: A weighing scale, also known as a balance or mass scale, is a device designed to measure the mass or weight of an object by determining the gravitational force acting upon it and comparing it to a known standard. These instruments operate on principles of equilibrium or force transduction, converting the applied load into a readable value in units such as grams, kilograms, pounds, or ounces. The history of weighing scales spans over 5,000 years, originating in ancient Mesopotamia during the mid-third millennium BC with the use of standardized stone weights for trade and exchange. By around 3000 BC, equal-arm lever balances had emerged independently in Egypt and Mesopotamia, allowing for precise comparisons by balancing unknown masses against sets of calibrated weights. These early devices held cultural significance, symbolizing justice in Egyptian, Grecian, Roman, and Jewish traditions, where the balance represented fairness in judgment and trade. Key innovations followed, including the unequal-arm steelyard in ancient Greece by the fifth century BC and its widespread adoption in the Roman Empire by the first century CE, which improved efficiency for larger loads through variable arm lengths. The spring scale, invented in 1770 by Richard Salter, marked a shift from purely mechanical balances to elastic force measurement, paving the way for platform and industrial scales in the 19th century. By the 20th century, electronic load cell technology and digital displays revolutionized accuracy and usability, evolving into smart scales integrated with health monitoring by the 2010s. Weighing scales encompass diverse types tailored to specific applications, broadly categorized into mechanical, spring-based, and electronic varieties. Mechanical balances, such as the classic two-pan equal-arm design, rely on levers and fulcrums for equilibrium without external power. Spring or load-cell scales use deformation of elastic elements to gauge force, suitable for everyday and industrial use. Digital and analytical balances employ strain gauges or electromagnetic force restoration for high precision, often achieving resolutions down to 0.1 mg in laboratory settings. Specialized forms include platform scales for heavy loads, jewelry scales for fine measurements, and medical scales for body weight assessment. In modern contexts, weighing scales are indispensable across commerce, manufacturing, healthcare, and scientific research, ensuring fair trade and reliable data. Legal metrology standards, such as those outlined in the NIST Handbook 44, specify tolerances, accuracy classes (from Class I for ultra-precise lab use to Class III for general commercial applications), and testing procedures to maintain measurement integrity. These regulations, adopted internationally through bodies like the International Organization of Legal Metrology (OIML), protect consumers by verifying that scales used in transactions accurately reflect quantities for billing or sale. Advances in sensor technology continue to enhance portability, connectivity, and automation, with scales now often featuring wireless data transfer and integration with inventory systems.
